title: How to choose between a 401(k), IRA, and taxable brokerage account
description: The 'Order of Operations' for filling your investment buckets efficiently.
content:
Investing is not just about *what* you buy (stocks vs bonds), but *where* you hold it. The US government offers a menu of account types—401(k), 403(b), Roth IRA, Traditional IRA, HSA, Taxable Brokerage—each with its own rules, limits, and tax superpowers. Choosing the wrong account can lock up your money for decades or cause you to miss out on thousands of dollars in free tax breaks. This guide provides the definitive 'Waterfall' strategy for funding these accounts in the mathematically optimal order.

Key Takeaways

  • Free Money First: Always prioritize the employer match in your 401(k). It is a guaranteed 100% return on investment.
  • Tax-Free Growth Second: HSAs and Roth IRAs are the most powerful vehicles because the growth is never taxed. Prioritize these over taxable accounts.
  • Liquidity Last: Taxable brokerage accounts offer no tax breaks, but offer total liquidity. Fill this bucket only after tax-advantaged space is used up (or for specific pre-retirement goals).
  • The HSA Secret: The Health Savings Account is the only 'Triple Tax Advantaged' account in the code. It beats even the Roth IRA.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Unlike many countries with a single pension system, the US system is a patchwork. High earners often 'fill up' one bucket and spill over into the next. In 2025, the limits are roughly: 401(k) $23,500, IRA $7,000, HSA $4,300. Knowing these caps is essential for planning.

The Investment Hierarchy (The Waterfall)

Imagine pouring water into a series of buckets. You fill the top one until it overflows, then the next. Follow this order.

Bucket 1: 401(k) Match (The Free Lunch)

Goal: Contribution % needed to get full match.

Why: Instant 50-100% return. Risk-free. Never skip this.

Bucket 2: HSA (The Super-Roth)

Goal: Maximize ($4,300 individual / $8,550 family).

Why: Tax deduction IN, Tax-free growth, Tax-free OUT (for medical). If you don't use it for medical, it turns into a traditional IRA at age 65. It is the best account in existence.

Bucket 3: Roth IRA (The Tax-Free Shelter)

Goal: Maximize ($7,000).

Why: Tax-free growth and flexibility. You can withdraw contributions anytime. Better investment options than 401(k).

Bucket 4: Remaining 401(k) (The Tax Deflector)

Goal: Maximize ($23,500).

Why: Reduces your current year taxable income significantly.

Bucket 5: Taxable Brokerage (The Overflow)

Goal: Unlimited.

Why: No limits, total liquidity. Use this for early retirement (FIRE) bridges or large purchases (House).

Decision Nuances

  1. High Fees Exception: If your 401(k) has terrible fees (1%+), only contribute up to the match. Then switch immediately to your IRA (where you control the fees). Only go back to the 401(k) if you still have money left over.
  2. Early Retirement Goal: If you plan to retire at 45, you need more money in Bucket 5 (Taxable) because Buckets 1-4 are age-restricted. You might intentionally skip filling the 401(k) to build a liquid bridge fund.
  3. Income Limits: If you earn too much for a Roth IRA (>$165k single), use the 'Backdoor Roth' method to bypass the limit legally.

Frequently Asked Questions

What about a Traditional IRA?

If you have a 401(k) at work, the tax deduction for a Traditional IRA phases out at higher incomes. Therefore, for most employed people, the Roth IRA or Backdoor Roth is the only logical choice for the IRA bucket.

Can I have both a 401(k) and an IRA?

Yes! You can (and should) have both. They have separate contribution limits. $23,500 for the 401(k) + $7,000 for the IRA = $30,500 total space.

When can I withdraw from Taxable?

Anytime. Tomorrow. There are no age restrictions. You just pay Capital Gains tax on the profit. It is the most flexible account, just the least tax-efficient.
